approaches.name: Antegrade femoral nailing through a piriformis entry
approaches.corridor: Proximal gluteal split aligned with the femoral bow to a piriformis-fossa start just medial to the greater-trochanter tip

sources.title: Antegrade nailing approach with piriformis entry point
Antegrade Nailing Approach With Piriformis Entry Point
Piriformis versus trochanteric entry points for femoral antegrade nailing

procedure_applications.condition: An antegrade straight nail is selected and proximal anatomy permits a collinear piriformis-fossa start

positioning.text: Position supine or lateral according to reduction strategy, with the pelvis accessible and the hip positioned to obtain true AP and lateral images of the proximal femur.

setup.text: Drape to the pelvic rim, plan reduction and traction, and verify that imaging can show the piriformis start, neck, canal, fracture, and distal femur before incision.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the greater-trochanter tip, femoral axis, projected anatomic bow, and pelvic rim, using fluoroscopy when habitus obscures palpation.

incision.text: Make a 3–5 cm incision generally 10–15 cm proximal to the trochanter tip, farther proximal when habitus requires, aligned with the proximal extension of the femoral bow rather than horizontally.

superficial_interval.text: Open fascia in line with the incision and split gluteal fibers longitudinally, maintaining a collinear soft-tissue path to bone.

deep_interval.text: Palpate the trochanter and place the guidewire at the piriformis fossa just medial to the trochanter tip under AP and lateral fluoroscopy.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia lata/gluteal fascia, gluteal muscle split, piriformis-fossa cortex, then femoral canal.

structures_encountered.text: Gluteal fascia and muscle, greater trochanter, piriformis-fossa region, proximal femoral cortex, neck-adjacent bone, and medullary canal define the entry.

structures_at_risk.text: The superior gluteal nerve and vessels, femoral-neck cortex, abductor tissue, proximal femoral cortex, and posterior shaft cortex are at risk from a noncollinear track.

danger_zones.text: A too-distal skin portal or oblique guidewire causes eccentric reaming, medial cortical blowout, posterior perforation, or iatrogenic femoral-neck fracture.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid forceful lateral retraction that bends the soft-tissue track; lengthen the incision proximally to achieve collinearity rather than levering instruments against the trochanter.

exposure.text: Provides a direct start for straight antegrade nails aligned closely with the femoral canal while limiting fracture-site exposure.

limitations.text: The piriformis start can be technically difficult in obesity and demands precise positioning; comparative trials do not show universal clinical superiority over trochanteric entry.

extensions.text: Extend the proximal skin and muscle split to restore a collinear trajectory; use a reduction window at the fracture only when closed methods fail.

indications.text: Use for selected femoral shaft or distal-third fractures treated with a compatible straight antegrade nail and a safe piriformis start.

relative_contraindications.text: Favor another entry when body habitus, proximal anatomy, prior implants, hip disease, or nail design prevents safe collinear piriformis access.

implant_implications.text: Use only a nail designed for piriformis entry and maintain the guidewire, opening reamer, and nail along the canal to avoid neck or cortical stress.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm the start and guidewire on true AP and lateral views, then monitor centered reaming, fracture alignment, nail depth, and proximal and distal locking.

closure.text: Irrigate, confirm hemostasis, repair fascia without tethering abductors, and close subcutaneous tissue and skin.

complications.text: Complications include superior-gluteal or abductor injury, hip pain, eccentric reaming, trochanteric or neck fracture, cortical perforation, malalignment, nonunion, and infection.

bailouts.text: If the start cannot be made collinear, stop repeated reaming, reposition or extend proximally, or change to a compatible trochanteric or retrograde strategy.

questions.question: Where is the piriformis entry point?
questions.answer: Just medial to the tip of the greater trochanter and aligned with the femoral canal.

questions.question: Why is a distal skin incision dangerous?
questions.answer: It creates an oblique track that promotes eccentric reaming and cortical or femoral-neck injury.

approaches.name: Antegrade femoral nailing through a trochanteric entry
approaches.corridor: Proximal gluteal split aligned with the femoral bow to a centered start at the greater-trochanter tip

sources.title: Antegrade nailing approach with trochanteric entry point
Antegrade Nailing Approach With Trochanteric Entry Point
Piriformis versus trochanteric entry points for femoral antegrade nailing

procedure_applications.condition: A proximally curved antegrade nail is selected and a centered greater-trochanter start matches implant design

positioning.text: Position supine or lateral with the pelvis accessible and obtain true AP and axial/lateral images of the greater trochanter and proximal femur.

setup.text: Drape to the pelvic rim, plan reduction and traction, and verify imaging from the trochanter through the distal femur before incision.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the trochanter tip, femoral axis, projected bow, and pelvic rim using fluoroscopy when necessary.

incision.text: Make a 3–5 cm incision about 10–15 cm proximal to the trochanter tip, farther proximal in obesity, along the proximal extension of the femoral bow.

superficial_interval.text: Open fascia and split gluteal fibers longitudinally, maintaining a direct soft-tissue track aligned with the femoral shaft.

deep_interval.text: Palpate the trochanter and establish a guidewire start adjacent to its tip on AP view and exactly centered on the axial view.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, gluteal fascia, longitudinal gluteal split, trochanteric cortex, then femoral canal.

structures_encountered.text: Gluteal fascia and muscle, abductor insertion region, greater trochanter, proximal cortex, and femoral canal define the approach.

structures_at_risk.text: The superior gluteal nerve, abductor tissue, anterior and posterior trochanteric walls, femoral neck, and posterior shaft cortex are at risk.

danger_zones.text: An off-center axial start or distal skin portal produces anterior/posterior trochanter blowout, eccentric reaming, medial cortical weakening, or neck stress.

retraction_hazards.text: Do not lever instruments against the trochanter to compensate for a distal incision; extend proximally until the soft-tissue track is collinear.

exposure.text: Provides a relatively accessible start for proximally curved antegrade nails with limited fracture-site dissection.

limitations.text: The start must match nail geometry and be centered axially; a nominally easier portal does not tolerate imprecise positioning.

extensions.text: Extend the incision proximally for collinearity or add a limited fracture reduction window if closed reduction fails.

indications.text: Use for selected shaft and distal-third fractures treated with a compatible proximally curved antegrade nail.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose another portal or strategy when proximal anatomy, previous implants, abductor pathology, habitus, or nail design prevents a safe centered start.

implant_implications.text: Use a nail specifically designed for trochanteric entry and keep wire, opening reamer, and nail centered through the trochanter into the canal.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Verify the start on AP and axial/lateral views, then monitor centered reaming, fracture alignment, nail depth, and locking.

closure.text: Irrigate, repair fascia without abductor tethering, and close subcutaneous tissue and skin.

complications.text: Complications include abductor injury and hip pain, trochanteric blowout, femoral-neck stress fracture, cortical perforation, malalignment, nonunion, and infection.

bailouts.text: If a centered track cannot be established, stop repeated opening attempts, reposition or extend the exposure, or change to another compatible nailing strategy.

questions.question: Where must the trochanteric start lie on axial imaging?
questions.answer: Exactly centered on the greater trochanter and aligned with the canal.

questions.question: Which nail geometry uses this portal?
questions.answer: A proximally curved antegrade nail designed for trochanteric entry.

questions.question: What can an eccentric start cause?
questions.answer: Trochanteric wall blowout, eccentric reaming, malalignment, or femoral-neck stress.

approaches.name: Retrograde femoral nailing through the intercondylar notch
approaches.corridor: Small infrapatellar medial-paratendinous or transpatellar route to an intercondylar start aligned with Blumensaat line

sources.title: Retrograde nailing versus distal femoral plating
Optional entry point for retrograde femoral nailing

procedure_applications.condition: A distal femoral or selected shaft fracture is suitable for retrograde fixation and the knee and implant environment permit intercondylar entry

positioning.text: Position supine with the knee flexed about 30 degrees over a radiolucent support, allowing true AP and lateral imaging from the notch through the fracture.

setup.text: Prep the full limb, assess knee contamination and prior implants, plan reduction, and verify that the intercondylar notch and Blumensaat line are visible.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark patellar borders, inferior pole, patellar tendon, tibial plateau, joint line, femoral axis, and fluoroscopic Blumensaat line.

incision.text: Make an approximately 2-cm longitudinal midline incision just distal to the inferior patellar pole over the patellar tendon.

superficial_interval.text: Spread medial parapatellar tissues longitudinally and gently retract the patellar tendon laterally, or use a controlled tendon split when indicated.

deep_interval.text: Enter the intercondylar notch at the canal axis: centered on AP and in line with Blumensaat line laterally, anterior and lateral to the PCL femoral attachment.

layers.text: Skin, infrapatellar soft tissue, medial paratendinous interval or tendon split, joint capsule and synovium, intercondylar cartilage entry, then distal femoral canal.

structures_encountered.text: Patellar tendon, infrapatellar fat and synovium, trochlear/intercondylar cartilage, ACL and PCL attachment regions, notch, and distal femoral canal are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: ACL, PCL attachment, weight-bearing cartilage, patellar tendon, tibial plateau, and popliteal neurovascular structures are at risk.

danger_zones.text: A start posterior to Blumensaat line threatens the ACL, an anterior or off-center start injures cartilage or drives malalignment, and uncontrolled posterior plunging threatens the popliteal bundle.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract the patellar tendon gently and avoid levering sleeves against cartilage; adjust knee flexion rather than forcing the guidewire past patella or tibial plateau.

exposure.text: Provides direct access from the intercondylar notch into the distal femoral canal with minimal fracture-site dissection.

limitations.text: The approach violates the knee joint and may contribute to anterior knee pain; the wide metaphyseal canal can permit varus-valgus or sagittal malalignment.

extensions.text: Enlarge the parapatellar interval for direct notch visualization or add limited fracture reduction and blocking techniques when metaphyseal alignment cannot be controlled.

indications.text: Use for selected distal femoral and shaft fractures, including compatible periprosthetic patterns, when sufficient distal bone and an accessible intercondylar box permit stable fixation.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid with active knee sepsis, incompatible femoral components or closed box, inadequate distal segment, open contaminated knee injury, or articular anatomy preventing a safe start.

implant_implications.text: Select nail length and distal fixation for the fracture and any arthroplasty stem, countersink the nail beneath cartilage, and use blocking strategies when the metaphyseal canal does not guide alignment.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Every start-point step requires AP and lateral fluoroscopy; verify central notch entry, Blumensaat alignment, fracture length and axes, nail depth, and locking-screw safety.

closure.text: Irrigate the knee thoroughly to remove drilling debris, repair tendon or paratendinous tissues and capsule, and close skin in layers.

complications.text: Complications include ACL or cartilage injury, knee pain and stiffness, septic arthritis, patellar-tendon injury, malalignment, popliteal injury, nonunion, and hardware prominence.

bailouts.text: If the start cannot be proven safe or the distal segment cannot be aligned, stop reaming, improve direct visualization and reduction, add blocking fixation, or convert to plating.

questions.question: Where is the retrograde start on the lateral view?
questions.answer: In line with Blumensaat line, not posterior to it.

questions.question: Where is it relative to the PCL attachment?
questions.answer: Anterior and lateral to the proximal PCL attachment.

questions.question: Why is about 30 degrees of knee flexion used?
questions.answer: Less flexion lets the tibial plateau obstruct entry; greater flexion brings the patella and articular surface into danger.
